title: Let Chaos Reign, and Then Rein In Chaos | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: Andreessen argues that chaotic bottom-up entry is the signature of consequential technologies, as with PCs, spreadsheets and email, and that agents will follow the same path. The winners are firms that build a 'habitat' reining in agent chaos just enough, becoming self-driving companies.

insights.claim: A reliable tell that a technology will actually change the world is that it enters workplaces chaotically, bottom-up, rather than through sanctioned IT rollout.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Use bottom-up, unsanctioned adoption as a leading indicator when screening enterprise tech and AI products.
insights.quote: One of the best tells that a technology will actually change the world is, “Does it make a chaotic entrance?”
insights.locator: Chaos! It's one of the most underrated

insights.claim: Chaos signals that employees have staked a claim on something they find immediately valuable and aligned with their own ability to contribute, so it reveals real demand rather than noise.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Grassroots usage is stronger evidence of product-market fit than top-down purchase.

insights.claim: The key question after a chaotic entrance, per Andy Grove, is who will let chaos reign and then rein it in, implying the durable value accrues to whoever builds the governing layer.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Look for companies selling the control/governance layer around bottom-up AI adoption.
insights.quote: who is going to let chaos reign, and then rein in the chaos?
insights.locator: Chaos! It's one of the most underrated

insights.claim: Personal computers arrived at work because employees brought them in and plugged them in regardless of permission, with some falsifying procurement forms as oscilloscopes, typewriters or desks, much like ChatGPT's workplace entry a few years ago.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: The ChatGPT-style shadow adoption pattern repeats a well-documented PC-era precedent.
insights.quote: People lied on their procurement forms, claiming they were buying an oscilloscope, or a typewriter, or even a desk.

insights.claim: A 1983 article warned that PCs would create 'shadow' data processing departments hidden from top management, and IT reacted by trying to regain control, yet smart leaders recognized the behavior as valuable.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Initial IT/security backlash is the expected reaction and not a sign the technology will fail.
insights.quote: “shadow” data processing departments that perform corporate calculations hidden from top management’s view

insights.claim: Spreadsheets were arguably the original workplace agent, letting non-programmers model, calculate and project their business, and drove demand for PCs as the PC's killer app.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Frames agents as the same class of end-user empowerment tool, supporting a long adoption runway.

insights.claim: Rogue spreadsheets were the analog of rogue agents: real-looking business artifacts that were often hallucinations, poorly documented, error-ridden and understood only by their creator.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Ungoverned agent output carries similar audit and error risk, which creates demand for auditing tooling.

insights.claim: Spreadsheet chaos was resolved with a habitat of data access rules, cell locking conventions, version histories, standardized formulas and output auditing, after which spreadsheets became indispensable.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: The governance checklist for spreadsheets maps to what agent platforms must ship: permissions, versioning, audit.

insights.claim: Email initially threatened executive control because the mailroom had governed who could reach whom, prompting proposals that sending email require managerial approval, before permissioned and access-controlled communication habitats emerged.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Control-anxiety proposals (approval gates) historically lost to permissioning, a hint for how agent policy will resolve.
insights.quote: It was considered a reasonable idea, for a minute, to have to get managerial approval to send an email.

insights.claim: Two lessons from computing history: someone must rein in chaos a little and create a habitat for the behavior to thrive, and the chaos itself indicates valuable behavior that builds deep alignment inside the company.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Core framework for evaluating agent infrastructure: enable then govern, not block.
insights.locator: So there are two lessons here

insights.claim: Over-control is as wrong as no control: agent and code creation should be 'free-range', neither caged nor fully free, because excess restriction kills the bottom-up enthusiasm and ownership that drives productivity.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Products that cage agents risk rejection; those that let them roam inside guardrails win.
insights.quote: You don’t want to put it in a cage. Nor do you want to let it run completely free. But you want it free-range.

insights.claim: Today most agents run in chat windows, personal accounts and one-off scripts with whatever credentials and data they were handed, with no one deciding what they can touch or seeing what they did.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Credential sprawl and lack of observability for agents is the gap that agent-governance products target.
insights.quote: Nobody decided what they could touch, and nobody can see what they did.
insights.locator: One thing I love about Amjad

themes.theme: Productivity and alignment from empowered individuals

insights.claim: People who already know what needs doing become radically more productive first when disruptive tools arrive, with 100x claimed, and there is no substitute for them.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Value accrues to domain-knowledgeable employees paired with agents, not to generic headcount.
insights.quote: There is no substitute for these people.

insights.claim: A Sumitomo Mitsui Finance and Leasing employee reportedly used Replit to do in one week a development process meant to take six people six months, as cited by the author from memory.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Anecdotal customer proof point for Replit's enterprise traction; roughly 25x in person-time terms and unverified.
insights.quote: I believe Replit has an example where one employee at Sumitomo Mitsui Finance and Leasing

insights.claim: Business success depends on how well individuals translate personal alignment with the business into whole-organization alignment through the artifacts they produce and the followers they attract.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Alignment, not tool count, is the scarce variable; bottom-up artifacts drive org-wide direction.

themes.theme: Code as aligning artifact and the self-driving company

insights.claim: Code is the ultimate aligning artifact because it literally is the organization's business logic, but generating it bottom-up by many new people is inherently chaotic.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Widening who can write code makes governance of code and agents a core enterprise software category.

insights.claim: Nothing creates alignment like expanding the opportunity set of who can contribute code, and a company must become aligned to become self-driving.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Supports demand for no-/low-code agent builders (Replit-like) inside enterprises.
insights.quote: nothing creates alignment quite like expanding the opportunity set of who can contribute code

insights.claim: Soon a company's alignment will be measurable by the richness of its agent habitat, and self-driving companies will pull ahead of most companies that do not yet get this.
insights.speaker: Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: Expect a performance gap between agent-rich and agent-poor firms; agent habitat depth could become a diligence metric.
insights.quote: Soon, you’ll be able to measure a company’s alignment by the richness of its agent habitat.
